What is at stake is the redefinition of the material boundaries of the user's sovereignty over their own equipment.<1>p. 521</1>

The case of the Vanguard anti-cheat exposes, in a particularly clear way, a qualitative mutation in the private governance of the immaterial object of consumption. It is no longer only a matter of conditioning the enjoyment of the game on internal rules of conduct, progression or permanence in the ecosystem, but of projecting the requirements of competitive integrity onto the consumer's own material infrastructure.<1>p. 520-521</1>

In the official support communications devoted to League of Legends and VALORANT, Riot itself describes Vanguard as security software composed of a client active while the game is running and a kernel-mode driver, that is, installed in the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system, with access far greater than that of ordinary applications <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</2>.<3>p. 521</3>

In the case of League of Legends, Riot makes explicit that Vanguard must remain active not only during the match, but also whenever the client is open, and that its deactivation, uninstallation or unauthorized interaction prevents use of the game; in the case of VALORANT, it further states that deactivating the system requires restarting the machine to restore the possibility of playing <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</2>.<3>p. 521</3>

In an official update published at the end of 2025, Riot makes even more explicit the logic of preventive governance that sustains Vanguard. The text states that the company identified a critical flaw in several modern motherboards, capable of allowing the invisible injection of code in the very initial stages of the machine's startup, even before the operating system has fully loaded. On the basis of this finding, Riot justifies the hardening of its integrity requirements by arguing that components loaded earlier in the boot process operate with a higher degree of privilege and, precisely for that reason, can compromise the entire environment before the operating system or the anti-cheat itself can react. The document also clarifies that, given this breach, Vanguard's restriction service may prevent VALORANT from running until the user updates the motherboard firmware or enables certain security layers deemed necessary by the platform.<1>p. 522</1>

Riot contractually admits the possibility of actively monitoring the use of its services not only on its own servers, but also on the consumer's computer or device, and provides that the anti-cheat software may keep running in the background on the device. As a result, the protection of the IOC does not remain confined to the concrete moment of the match. It becomes a vector of preventive and continuing governance over the technical environment in which the game will run, reaching the machine even before the specific decision to enjoy it.<1>p. 521-522</1>
The user's computer is, functionally, administered as an extension of the game's competitive environment.<1>p. 527</1>

Riot itself, in documents aimed at VALORANT developers and users, admits that Vanguard may block third-party applications, require sensitive changes to BIOS or UEFI, and require TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, IOMMU, memory integrity and other security layers to be enabled, and it recognizes that incorrect changes to these settings may cause serious problems on the computer.<1>p. 526-527</1>

These are the acronyms for Basic Input/Output System and Unified Extensible Firmware Interface. They designate the basic software interfaces that reside in the hardware and are responsible for preparing the machine to start the operating system.<1>p. 527</1>

On its system restrictions page, Riot expressly admits that it may limit access to the games when it identifies machines considered excessively prone to cheating, including because of outdated versions of Windows or specific equipment configurations, requiring the user to make sensitive changes to BIOS or UEFI, that is, to the machine's basic startup systems, such as enabling TPM 2.0 (a security module used for integrity verification and protected key storage), Secure Boot (a mechanism that prevents untrusted components from starting), IOMMU (a technology that isolates device access to memory) and memory integrity mechanisms, as well as updating the BIOS and the operating system itself <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025q)</2>.<3>p. 527</3>

Even more concretely, the guidance on incompatible software clarifies that Vanguard may prevent VALORANT from running when it identifies “.sys” files, that is, low-level drivers responsible for communication between the operating system and functions or components of the computer, instructing the user to remove the related software or even to manually delete the blocked file; among the examples mentioned by Riot itself are old drivers, outdated monitoring tools and RGB lighting control programs<1>p. 527</1>

The platform makes the enjoyment of the immaterial object conditional on the prior conformity of the machine's technical ecosystem with private standards of integrity and compatibility that it defines unilaterally.<1>p. 527</1>

In an effort to constantly improve the Riot Services, promote the evolution of our games and keep the Riot Services safe, fun and protected, you agree that we may alter, modify, update, suspend, “nerf” or restrict your access to any features or parts of the Riot Services, including Virtual Products (for example, we may alter some features of Virtual Products for regulatory or legal reasons or to improve the game experience) and we may require you to download and install software and updates of any software necessary to support the Riot Services, at any time, without liability to you, to the extent permitted by law.<1>p. 526</1>

You also understand and agree that these changes or updates to the Riot Services may change the system specifications needed to play our games and, in that case, you, and not Riot Games, will be responsible for purchasing any additional software or hardware needed to access and play our games.<1>p. 526</1>

In parallel, the contractual wording seeks to reduce the supplier's patrimonial exposure by stating that the services are offered as is, without broad warranties, assigning to the user responsibility for use and limiting Riot's liability for losses and damages, including in relation to failures linked to not installing updates or to maintaining minimum system requirements.<1>p. 526</1>

The general contractual framework thus seeks to provide in advance for subjecting the consumer's equipment to additional layers of surveillance, compulsory adaptation and risk shifting. This is the point at which the case stops being only a discussion about fighting cheating and becomes a classic problem of a supplier using the contract to shield itself in the face of an invasive technical architecture that it imposes itself.<1>p. 526</1>

Under the vocabulary of security, this expansion usually appears as if it were simple technical inevitability. But the discourse of security does not, by itself, neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture adopted.<1>p. 522</1>

In the digital environment, the storage, sharing and persistent monitoring of information pose a threat to privacy serious enough to require specific normative containment, especially in a surveillance society in which data processing becomes a central asset of business models and of behavioral control <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69; p. 73; p. 82)</2>. The security argument itself can serve to legitimize the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life, especially when the demand for data and structural surveillance are normalized through routine and barely intelligible acceptances<3>p. 522-523</3>

It is not enough, therefore, to invoke fighting cheating as a magic word. The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the degree of technical interference demanded of the consumer.<1>p. 523</1>

Monitoring technologies and algorithmic governance embody human choices and restructure power relations over the user, allowing veiled control and the favoring of their own interests by those who dominate the digital infrastructure<1>p. 523</1>

When organized data function as operational substitutes for the person, surveillance ceases to be a simple administrative instrument and becomes a potential mechanism for affecting individuality, autonomy and the free development of personality<1>p. 524-525</1>

Even if the agent remains private, the intensification of control over hardware, informational flows and practical conditions of use remains subject to the protective filter that radiates from the Constitution over the entire legal order <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 205; p. 531)</2>. The constitutional order remains in the room precisely because the platform does not act only on an abstract thing, but on the consumer's practical sphere, their equipment, their privacy and their real possibility of enjoying or not enjoying the object without subjecting the rest of the machine to mutable private standards of integrity.<3>p. 525-526</3>
Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security.<1>p. 533</1>

Products and services placed on the market cannot entail risks to health or safety beyond those that are normal and foreseeable given their nature and enjoyment, and the supplier cannot place into circulation a product or service that it knows or should know to present a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness. In extreme cases, the very liability for design defects or for insufficient or inadequate information about use and risks reopens the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product.<1>p. 532-533</1>

The data processing linked to Vanguard cannot be justified en bloc under the generic heading of “security”, because it must observe a legitimate, specific, explicit and informed purpose, necessity, with limitation to the indispensable minimum, and transparency, with clear, precise and accessible information. It also requires an adequate legal basis, is not automatically satisfied by ritualized and generic acceptances, and presupposes technical and administrative measures capable of effectively protecting the data. In other words, the platform cannot invoke security as an all-encompassing justification while maintaining opacity about the scope, necessity and agents of the processing.<1>p. 533</1>

“Art. 6 [...] VI - transparency: guarantee, to data subjects, of clear, precise and easily accessible information about the carrying out of the processing and the respective processing agents, subject to commercial and industrial secrets;” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]a)</2>.<3>p. 533</3>
BRASIL. Lei nº 13.709, de 14 de agosto de 2018. Dispõe sobre a proteção de dados pessoais e altera a Lei nº 12.965, de 23 de abril de 2014 (Marco Civil da Internet).<1>p. 806</1>

Taken together, the sources are empirically valuable because they show, in the supplier's own institutional voice and in more than one game ecosystem, that the competitive protection of the IOC is implemented through deep technical access, early loading and structural permanence in the consumer's computing environment [...]<1>p. 521</1>

In specialized press coverage, the controversy revolved around the always-on character of the anti-cheat, its kernel-level loading from system startup, the fear of persistent surveillance and interference with non-game uses of the equipment. The value of this material lies not in proving any expert thesis on its own, but in showing that the criticism did not arise as fringe paranoia.<1>p. 527-528</1>

In reports hosted on Microsoft Q&A, a technically more reliable environment than scattered community forums, episodes of blue screens, serious crashes and systemic instability associated with the technical ecosystem in which Vanguard operates appear repeatedly<1>p. 529</1>

[...] although the technical answer does not attribute conclusive causality to Vanguard and mentions competing hypotheses, such as graphics driver failures, corrupted system files and a possible RAM defect, the report remains relevant as plausible support for the view that low-level, automatically starting software may be part of the practical horizon of an overall degradation of the equipment's stability<1>p. 529-530</1>

Even more concretely, community reports illustrate the conflict between Vanguard and legitimate, ordinary, non-game uses of the computer. They describe incompatibilities with hardware monitoring and management software, interference with study routines and conflicts with legitimate system debugging tools. Although they have only illustrative value, these sources are empirically useful because they materialize something central to the dogmatics of the case<1>p. 530</1>

Even the most extreme reports of possible bricking or severe loss of the equipment's availability are illustratively useful for the argument, even though they do not support conclusive expert claims.<1>p. 531</1>

Of course, the post neither proves conclusive technical causality nor allows one to state, by itself, that Vanguard “caused” definitive physical or logical damage to the hardware; its value is illustrative.<1>p. 532</1>
A term derived from "brick", used to describe the functional destruction or permanent disabling of a hardware component.<1>p. 531</1>

It is the extreme form of the problem. Not the only one, nor necessarily the most frequent, but the one that makes it impossible to pretend that we are only talking about “just another piece of game software”.<1>p. 532</1>
The argument does not depend on absolute demonstration of universal harm; it is enough to show that the required architecture transfers to the consumer a legally relevant systemic risk.<1>p. 530</1>

The most important point here is comparative: the kernel-level always-on architecture does not appear as an inevitable fact of every anti-cheat, but as a technical choice that intensifies the degree of intrusion, dependence and risk assumed by the consumer in the name of the ecosystem's competitive integrity.<1>p. 529</1>

In a comparative text published on the Medium portal, the user Uoiyouiyouiy <1>(2026)</1> contrasts Vanguard with Easy Anti-Cheat to argue that the architecture adopted by Riot has historically been deeper and more aggressive, above all because the driver loads at kernel level right at system startup and remains as a privileged observation layer over the machine.<2>p. 527</2>

The text is also particularly relevant in recording that, after the accumulated controversies around deep access, potential failures and systemic costs of this model, Vanguard's own recent trajectory would indicate a movement to reduce its permanent residence in the kernel and to shift part of the detection layers to user mode (that is, to the ordinary space in which programs run, less privileged and less risky than the kernel)<1>p. 528</1>

It would also be dishonest not to acknowledge that, even among the harshest criticisms, there is a consistent technical-cultural discourse in defense of more invasive measures, according to which fighting cheats in competitive games involves an asymmetric contest and continuous escalation, which would make it understandable for the platform to adopt deep countermeasures. This counterpoint is useful because it prevents an easy caricature of the practice. The serious legal question was never whether there is a legitimate interest in preserving competitive integrity; of course there is. The question is a different one: whether this interest is enough to authorize, without reinforced control, the expansion of the supplier's technical power over the material base of the consumer's equipment.<1>p. 532</1>

As a counterpoint to the more critical readings of the case, a technical-cultural discourse also circulates according to which public resistance to Vanguard stems, at least in part, from an insufficient understanding of the structural dynamics of fighting cheats in competitive games, marked by an asymmetric contest and by the continuous escalation of cheating techniques that reach ever deeper into the system, which is why more invasive measures would be presented as a functionally justifiable cost of preserving competitive integrity <1>Rigney</1><2>(Rigney, 2024)</2>.<3>p. 532</3>

[...] the very community text that seeks to correct “misinformation” does not eliminate the central objections, recognizing as real problems the possibility of crashing or disabling computers, the restriction on customizations and the loss of compatibility with part of the user base, especially on Linux<1>p. 532</1>

In an institutional statement prepared by its security and privacy teams, Riot builds an explicit defense of Vanguard's invasive architecture against public criticism about privacy and security. The text seeks to justify kernel-level access on the argument that more sophisticated cheats no longer operate only in the ordinary space of software, but advance into deeper layers of the operating system; therefore, according to the company, an anti-cheat restricted to user mode would be technically insufficient to preserve so-called competitive integrity.<1>p. 522</1>

At the same time, the communication tries to reduce the perception of risk by maintaining that the driver does not, by itself, collect or transmit information from the user's computer and by highlighting internal and external security reviews, as well as a bounty program for identifying vulnerabilities.<1>p. 522</1>

[...] at the same time, the very existence of this counterpoint confirms that the dispute does not revolve around the nonexistence of costs, but around their justifiability, proportionality and acceptability in light of the competitive integrity sought by the platform <1>Rigney · SERTENSEAL</1><2>(Rigney, 2024; SerTenseal, [2024])</2>.<3>p. 532</3>
The recognition, however, does not eliminate the legal tensions, but only tends to make them more predictable.<1>p. 493</1>

The sectoral regulation of electronic games matters, above all, because it dismantles two bad simplifications: that the sector would be legally invisible and that naming it in legislation would be enough to resolve the central conflicts of its governance.<1>p. 543</1>

The legal framework for electronic games expressly recognizes the existence of an industry of its own, regulates its central economic chain — manufacturing, importation, commercialization, development and commercial use — and provides a normative definition of what counts as an electronic game, including interactive audiovisual works developed as a computer program, devices and accessories, and software consumed by download or streaming.<1>p. 543</1>

“Art. 11. [...] investment in the development of electronic games is considered investment in research, development, innovation and culture. Art. 12. The development of electronic games is considered a cultural segment for the purposes of Law No. 8,313/1991.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>.<3>p. 544</3>

The institutionalization of the sector matters because it reinforces, on the documentary record, the reading that games (above all under models operated as a service) are not limited to isolated products delivered in a single event. The offering takes shape as an ecosystem sustained by continuous operation, permanent updating and the enforcement of internal rules that are part of the material content of the supply.<1>p. 493</1>

What matters is to record the minimum context in which games operated as a service come to draw public and legal attention, highlighting vectors that reappear when enjoyment depends on an environment of continuous operation under intense private governance. Against this background, a twofold movement can be observed. On the one hand, there is an effort to institutionalize games as a relevant economic and cultural activity. On the other, concerns keep recurring about the protection of vulnerable audiences, monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, the processing of personal data, and market and advertising practices integrated into the very experience of enjoyment.<1>p. 493</1>

The recognition of the sector as a relevant economic and cultural activity coexists with predictable focal points linked to the protection of children and adolescents, to monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, to the processing of personal data and to market and advertising practices integrated into the environment of enjoyment. These vectors do not appear as episodic accidents, but as typical effects of ecosystems in which utility is realized over time, under private governance of the environment and through rules susceptible to unilateral modulation, with structural asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.<1>p. 496</1>
In games as a service, acquisition tends to occur continuously and in segments, embedded in the very experience of enjoyment.<1>p. 494</1>

The framework organizes the sector institutionally through principles and guidelines and, in the core most important for this thesis, affirms that electronic games must be conceived in light of respect for fundamental rights and democratic values, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents, and the preservation of privacy, the protection of personal data and informational self-determination. This perspective is decisive because it shows that the legal order already treats the sector as an economic and cultural activity crossed by multisectoral public concerns, and not as a playful enclave left solely to private enterprise. Its dogmatic relevance lies in preventing any attempt at legal infantilization of the problem, as if electronic games still belonged to the regulatory limbo of “it's just entertainment”.<1>p. 544-545</1>

Sole paragraph. Commercial promotions or lottery modalities regulated by Laws No. 13,756, of December 12, 2018, and 14,790, of December 29, 2023, or any type of game that offers some type of bet, with prizes in real or virtual assets, or that involves a random or forecast-based outcome, are not considered electronic games, and the companies and professionals involved in the production or distribution of these activities are prohibited from benefiting from any advantage defined in this Law.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>.<3>p. 544</3>

“Art. 2 The protection of rights relating to industrial property [...] is effected through: […] VI - granting of registration for electronic games.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]c)</2>.<3>p. 547</3>

By adding the granting of registration for electronic games to the Industrial Property Law, the legal framework shows that games have come to be considered, more robustly, an object of legal protection within the innovation economy. This matters for the thesis because it confirms that the legal order has assimilated the sector not only as a cultural and market activity, but also as a reality capable of radiating consequences into the regimes of exclusivity. The consequence, however, is not to turn intellectual property into the total language of the problem. On the contrary, it makes it even more necessary to contain the proprietarian temptation to capture entirely conflicts that, on the plane of enjoyment, remain conflicts of governed consumption.<1>p. 547</1>

The point of greatest sensitivity arises when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, often referred to in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what is acquired come to depend on internal regimes of distribution, availability criteria and limits defined by the platform, and are also linked to signals of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. Institutional discussion then tends to focus on minimum transparency of the conditions of acquisition, protection of vulnerable audiences and control of practices that induce consumption, not out of a desire to moralize the sector, but because the supplier concentrates internal criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, under conditions of low external reconstructibility.<1>p. 494-495</1>

In this context, Law No. 15,211/2025 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2> offers sufficient normative anchoring to situate the focal point by regulating, from the standpoint of protecting children and adolescents, the functionality of loot boxes as a mechanism for random acquisition upon payment. The interest of the statute, here, is evidential. Certain mechanics of the ecosystem have already been identified as structurally sensitive and, therefore, open to treatment by criteria. Under the IOC regime, such mechanisms condense elements such as instituted rarity, anticipation, criterial opacity and unilateral modulation, with effects that may manifest as material erosion of utility and reconfiguration of value, even if access remains formally available.<3>p. 495</3>

The protection of children and adolescents is one of these recurring vectors. Its centrality derives not only from concerns about content, but from the combination of interactivity, the permanence of the bond and exposure to acquisition and retention mechanisms built into the interfaces and rules of the environment. In games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to be fragmented over time, mediated by cycles of return, signals of urgency, promises of progression, social comparison and incentives embedded in the very design of enjoyment. The focus on minors thus works as an institutional trigger that brings to light asymmetries of understanding and of the capacity to contest in environments governed by architecture.<1>p. 494</1>
Sectoral normativity, therefore, already sees the games market as a place of sensitive monetization, behavioral shaping and informational vulnerability.<1>p. 545</1>
BRASIL. Lei nº 15.211, de 17 de setembro de 2025. Dispõe sobre a proteção de crianças e adolescentes em ambientes digitais (Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente).<1>p. 806</1>

The Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents reinforces this diagnosis by making explicit, on another normative front, that the digital environment is not neutral and that suppliers are subject to positive duties of prevention, protection, information and security. In this context, the very material content of the best interest of the child and adolescent already covers privacy, security, mental and physical health, access to information, freedom to participate in society and well-being. The norm goes beyond programmatic discourse by prohibiting loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents and banning profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising. In doing so, the legislator recognizes, head-on, that practices typical of the economic organization of electronic games may generate specific risks and deserve their own rules.<1>p. 545</1>

“Art. 20. Loot boxes offered in electronic games directed at children and adolescents are prohibited [...]. Art. 22. [...] the use of profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising is prohibited [...].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2>.<3>p. 545</3>

By prohibiting loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents, as well as in those likely to be accessed by this audience, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents did not merely recognize in the abstract the economic and behavioral sensitivity of this market, but began to interfere in the very way of organizing products that had previously been presented as fully compatible with the presence of minors in the digital ecosystem <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2>.<3>p. 545</3>

The statute imposes concrete duties to remove content that violates rights and requires a legal representative in the country with powers to receive service of process, while the regulating decree designates an administrative authority, provides for blocking orders and even triggers the technical infrastructural layer of the digital environment through coordination with Anatel and CGI.br. This is important because it dismantles the presentation of the platform as a self-sufficient sovereign space. The digital environment is already an object of public institutionality, with authorities, orders, enforcement mechanisms and mandatory points of contact. Pure self-regulation, in this scenario, poorly describes the state of the law in force.<1>p. 547</1>

“Art. 1 This Decree [...] designates the National Data Protection Agency - ANPD as autonomous administrative authority [...]. Art. 2 The ANPD is designated as the administrative authority [...]. Art. 3 The temporary suspension and the prohibition of the exercise of activities [...] shall be carried out by means of a blocking order.<1>p. 547</1>

BRASIL. Decreto nº 12.622, de 17 de setembro de 2025. Regulamenta a Lei nº 15.211, de 17 de setembro de 2025, para designar a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados como autoridade administrativa autônoma de proteção de crianças e adolescentes em ambientes digitais, e estabelecer competências para cumprimento de ordens judiciais de bloqueio.<1>p. 806</1>

Bringing its entry into force forward to March 2026 reinforces this point because it shows that the legislator did not treat the matter as a merely symbolic or deferrable agenda, but as a concrete regulatory problem, capable of requiring immediate adaptation by suppliers who structure their activity on microtransaction mechanisms and recurring capture of attention and spending <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]b)</2>.<3>p. 545-546</3>

Riot Games' institutional reaction to the new scenario shows, with particular clarity, both the strength and the limit of sectoral regulation. Instead of immediately reorganizing the economic architecture of League of Legends to keep its offer compatible with the continued presence of underage users, the company chose to shift the response to the level of access, stating that minors could not play titles rated 18+ (for those over eighteen) in Brazil, not even with the consent of their guardians, and tying any future restoration of enjoyment to the user's coming of age or to a future reclassification of the game's rating<1>p. 546</1>

In the “Riot Games Parents Portal”, the company clarifies that the guardian may manage account permissions, but not authorize a minor's access to an 18+ title; in addition, it states that accounts barred from accessing such games may remain frozen, with items, cosmetics, progress and other data linked to the user's history preserved until access is restored <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [2026]m)</2>. In other words, the business response neither deletes the account nor eliminates its digital collection, but separates the preservation of records from actual enjoyment, keeping the patrimonial and historical bond in a state of suspension.<3>p. 546</3>

The fact is dogmatically telling because it reveals, in an almost confessional way, that the value of the consumer relationship is not exhausted by the isolated act of acquisition, nor can it be reduced to the abstract ownership of digital records. What is in dispute is the continued enjoyment of a position built over time, whose utility depends on the user's continued presence in the governed environment.<1>p. 546</1>

The episode offers an especially valuable demonstration, since sectoral regulation proves capable of recognizing specific risks and of pressuring the market, but the private response is still organized according to the logic of the Lex Plataformae, that is, through the unilateral reengineering of the conditions of access and continued presence, and not through a spontaneous revision of the economic rationality that produced the problem. The result is revealing. Faced with a public norm aimed at protecting children and adolescents, the platform preserves the monetization model and shifts the practical cost of adaptation onto the vulnerable user, turning the former condition of tolerated and economically exploitable participant into one of temporary exclusion from the ecosystem.<1>p. 546-547</1>

The methodological importance of this picture lies in showing, with rare clarity, that the sectoral framing of the games market is indispensable, but not sufficient. It sees the risk, names the sector and produces relevant commands; it does not resolve, by itself, the dogmatic problem of continuous enjoyment subjected to opaque, mutable and unilaterally administered private governance.<1>p. 547</1>
The sectoral framework helps to see the market; it is not enough to control governance.<1>p. 548</1>

The Consumer Protection Code, in this frame, functions as a general grammar of protection in mass relationships marked by informational asymmetry and concentration of the power to organize the offer, without this anticipating, at this point, the specific dogmatic reconstruction of the IOC regime.<1>p. 496</1>

The offer is renewed through events, seasons, promotions, bundles and acquisition incentives built into use, so that advertising also operates as internal communication designed through storefronts, urgency messages, recommendations and highlighting mechanisms. This integration reinforces the continuous and mass character of the supply and tends to activate classic consumer protection instruments aimed at adequate information, transparency and control of abusive practices.<1>p. 495-496</1>

The central conflict remains elsewhere: in continued provision, in architectural opacity, in unilateral control of access, in relevant changes to enjoyment, in the modulation of visibility, in the administration of inventories, histories and reputations, in evidentiary asymmetry and in the private allocation of the conditions for remaining in the ecosystem. None of this disappears because the sector received a name and principles in a statute.<1>p. 548</1>

The existence of sectoral regulation does not replace the consumer-law infrastructure, nor does it authorize conflicts of enjoyment to be entirely absorbed by the grammar of the sector or by the language of innovation.<1>p. 548</1>

In IOCs, immaterial product and governed environment are dogmatically inseparable, and therefore the application of norms cannot be exhausted in the economic-cultural framing of the sector. It must reach administered enjoyment and the Lex Plataformae that organizes it. This insufficiency does not disqualify sectoral regulation. It only repositions its reach. The games framework, the protective digital statute and complementary normativity function as an important repertoire of recognition, public signaling of risks and institutional delimitation of the sector.<1>p. 548</1>

The sector may be recognized, promoted and legally named, and still the decisive question may remain open: which limits apply when the platform unilaterally reconfigures the access, use, visibility, continuity and functional equivalence of the immaterial object consumed? It is this question that the sectoral repertoire, alone, does not answer. And it is precisely for this reason that the protection of the IOC must be built not out of a fetish for the “games framework”, but out of the articulation between sectoral regulation, consumer protection, the constitutional economic order and limits on the private exercise of platform powers.<1>p. 548</1>
Free enterprise, innovation and technological ownership do not operate as safe-conducts for unauditability, shielded irresponsibility or contractual immunization of the supplier.<1>p. 512</1>

Private autonomy, in a constitutional key, is not an abstract safe-conduct for the user's material subjection, especially when inequality of power turns formal freedom into an elegant fiction <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183; p. 286)</2>. For this reason too, the reinforced application of fundamental rights in the private sphere does not depend on any rite of transforming the private party into a “quasi-State”; it is enough to recognize that the threat to liberty, material equality and dignity may come from holders of social and economic power intense enough to produce relevant subjection <3>Sarlet</3><4>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 527; p. 529; p. 530)</4>.<5>p. 515-516</5>

When the relationship between private parties is organized on non-equal terms, the purely formal invocation of contractual freedom is no longer enough to legitimize the bond, because the absence of overt coercion does not equal, by itself, the existence of real freedom to decide, resist or negotiate under minimally equivalent conditions <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183)</2>.<3>p. 515</3>

Free enterprise, in this picture, is neither a metaphysical right of capital nor a screen for business sovereignty, but a category functionally conditioned by constitutional purposes and by the protection of the person <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 204; p. 208-209)</2>.<3>p. 505-506</3>

When the technical environment reorganizes vulnerability at scale, legal reconstruction is not moralism, but a necessary response to keep the effects of new forms of power and intrusion controllable in institutional terms.<1>p. 348</1>
The platform need not be treated as a State for its powers to be subject to legal constraint.<1>p. 513</1>
At the same time, this containment does not require dissolving the private nature of the relationship nor transplanting the legal regime of the State in full to the private party.<1>p. 513</1>

Technical change structurally alters the conditions of exposure, harm and vulnerability, and requires categories to be adjusted so that protection stays true to the real way in which the conflict is produced. This does not imply equating platform with State nor constitutionalizing every private dispute, but recognizing that certain private powers, when exercised through architecture, information and enforcement at scale, generate asymmetries and risks that are not exhausted by the letter of the contract.<1>p. 348</1>
In a platform environment, this prevents the freedom to shape the bond from being turned into private sovereignty over the consumer's position.<1>p. 519</1>
The point here is not to automatically assert the total unlawfulness of the kernel anti-cheat, but to refuse its legal immunization.<1>p. 533</1>

It is not a matter of denying the legitimacy of fighting cheating, but of denying that this legitimacy authorizes, by itself, deep, preventive, persistent and opaque technical governance over someone else's machine.<1>p. 534</1>

The constitutionally legitimate market is one shaped by dignity, social function, the repression of abuse and consumer protection, and not one that tries to turn private architecture into an unchecked jurisdiction. From this matrix follows the dogmatic possibility of reconstructing, later on, platform governance as a legally controllable phenomenon and of reading the IOC not as an awkward exception to the system, but as one of its hardest contemporary tests.<1>p. 512</1>

The platform should not be naturalized as a simple medium, as if it were a neutral engineering unit to which the social would be added later.<1>p. 126</1>

From there, Feenberg formulates a highly productive premise for the legal critique of platforms: no technology is an island because every technology is mediated by markets and administrations.<1>p. 126</1>

If technology is always mediated by economic and administrative rationalities, then design choices must be read as socially situated decisions, open to criticism as to the purposes they fulfill and the asymmetries they produce, that is, as a locus of attribution and of assessment of legitimacy.<1>p. 126</1>

Non-neutrality does not present itself only as an abstract thesis. Feenberg observes that technically apparent arrangements of neutrality may incorporate unconscious preferences. In digital consumption, this has an immediate consequence, because the practical normativity of platforms (what becomes visible, recommendable, subjected to friction, permitted or rewarded) may operate as interface “naturalness”, masking value choices under the idiom of functionality.<1>p. 128</1>

Default patterns, hierarchies of choice, urgency devices and reward regimes guide conduct without needing to declare the value orientation that informs them. Even without a textual lie or omission, practical normativity can induce perceptions, desires and permanence through a grammar of interaction presented as simple usability.<1>p. 128</1>

Feenberg formulates the normative dimension of design by describing constraints materialized in systems capable of determining individual actions more effectively than political authority, bearing on reflexes, skills and attitudes <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36)</2>. When conduct is administered by systems and interfaces, governance ceases to operate only by explicit command and comes to operate by architecture. Platforms, in this sense, function as everyday governance, and legal responses cannot be restricted to clauses and notices when practical normativity is inscribed in the design <3>Feenberg</3><4>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</4>.<5>p. 128-129</5>

The passage from explicit command to architecture as governance allows us to distinguish a regime in which the consumer decides in the face of statements from another in which they decide within an environment that organizes microstructures of choice. This shift makes the purpose incorporated into design legally relevant. When constraints and incentives are integrated into the system to produce permanence, extraction and dependence under the appearance of enjoyment, teleology ceases to appear as a side effect and comes to compose the material form of supply <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</2>.<3>p. 129</3>
If the technical code is determined by actors, it is politically situated and economically orientable and, therefore, its teleologies can be reconstructed and criticized.<1>p. 135</1>

Feenberg asserts that the result of struggles and collaborations is a design code, that is, the stabilized intersection between social choice and technical specification <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 93)</2>. For the IOC regime, this is decisive because the consumed object is not reduced to the final content; it includes the set of mediations that makes this content enjoyable, monetizable and governable.<3>p. 129</3>

At the same time, the code can be critically assessed as to the purpose it fulfills, opening the way to the subsequent qualification of the teleology inscribed in architecture and governance.<1>p. 129-130</1>

Once stabilized, the code tends to reproduce itself through institutional inertia, path dependencies and legal and economic mechanisms that make alternatives and reappropriations more expensive. In this scenario, intellectual property appears as an infrastructure of semiotic and technical governance. It not only protects creations, but helps to delimit uses, restrict reconfigurations and consolidate the supplier's authority over the conditions of enjoyment, reinforcing the private character of the code that organizes the experience <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 93)</2>.<3>p. 130</3>

When the technical code defines conditions of enjoyment, permanence and loss, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer is not a mere informational defect, but architectural structure and, therefore, a field of legal relevance <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 101)</2>.<3>p. 136</3>

To prevent this critique from falling into a pessimistic substantivism, Feenberg anchors himself in a critical constructivism, according to which technology is neither value-neutral nor universal and, precisely for that reason, admits an explicit theory of democratic interventions in the technosystem <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 38)</2>.<3>p. 126</3>

“Democratic rationalization”, in Feenberg, is not a metaphor for “participation” in a generic sense. It is presented as a principle by which interventions of users and subordinate actors manage to impose on technical development needs that were ignored or to run against hierarchies already stabilized in the technical form.<1>p. 126</1>

Instead of participating individually as objects of a procedure, the activists act as an organized interested party and reorient the system toward new purposes, pressing for experimentation to become a standard form of care for the incurably ill and for the design of protocols to reflect, more responsively, the needs and urgencies of those who live with the condition.<1>p. 127</1>

The fact that the terminal “disguised itself” as a telephone device suggested to some users that the network could serve for interpersonal communication. From there, users “hacked” the network in which they were embedded and altered its functioning, introducing practices of online human communication, such as anonymous chat, aimed at fun, companionship and meetings, where mere data distribution had been planned.<1>p. 135</1>

First, the example shows that “democratic intervention” need not mean only external regulation; it can mean a dispute internal to the technical form and to the governance that administers it.<1>p. 127</1>

If technique is constructed and disputed, requirements such as open auditability and functional value equivalence can be read, from now on, as parameters for the democratization of design. They do not function as rhetorical ornaments of transparency, but as minimal material conditions so that the addressee is not reduced to the position of a mere executor of an architectural script oriented by extraction and organizational predictability <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 36-38)</2>.<3>p. 126-127</3>

The idea of democratic interventions in the technosystem is of objective interest because it allows us to understand legal criteria as forms of reorienting technical rationality without presupposing a “pure” externality of law.<1>p. 127</1>
Feenberg describes a mechanism by which ethical demands can be stabilized as technical requirements when they become legally enforceable.<1>p. 126</1>
Once materialized, the requirement ceases to circulate as moral debate and comes to form part of the technical regime of compliance and functioning.<1>p. 126</1>

In revisiting the theme of industrial labor, Feenberg exposes how the union of capital and science can be oriented toward reducing the workers' task to the exercise of vigilance and dexterity, reorganizing dependencies and reinforcing management's decision-making autonomy. Although the example is not digital, its function here is structural. It shows that technical decisions can be oriented by purposes of control and predictability and that this control materializes in technical form.<1>p. 133</1>

In formulating the notion of “operational autonomy”, Feenberg <1>(2002, p. 43)</1> seeks to demonstrate that capitalist control of the production process is not exercised only by legal-formal command or administrative coordination, but is consolidated when the very organization of labor is technically incorporated. It is at this point that the author turns to Karl Marx (citing an edition of Capital published in 1906) to argue that the specifically capitalist form of organizing the labor process comes to acquire a palpable technical reality insofar as machinery and productive arrangements turn the worker into a subordinate component of a preconstituted material system.<2>p. 133-134</2>

When this logic is transposed to consumption, the typical asymmetry of the technosystem appears as the supplier's operational autonomy. A successful architecture is one that reduces the operator's dependence on the subjects who use it, converts participation into data and value and does not generate an equivalent power to define purposes. In this scenario, consent tends to operate under material conditions of low contestability, because the consumer adheres to an operating regime whose rationality has already been decided and incorporated into the system, which deepens the distance between formal choice and practical governance <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 54-55)</2>.<3>p. 133-134</3>

The term “meta” is used in the technical sense of the competitive gaming ecosystem, as short for metagame. It is the set of dominant strategies, optimal choices and performance patterns stabilized in a given time frame, resulting from the interaction between rules, updates and the aggregate behavior of the community.<1>p. 121</1>

The English word “buff” designates a deliberate increase in the power and effectiveness of a game element (character, item, ability, system), with measurable impact on performance and on the metagame.<1>p. 121</1>

In League of Legends, buffs and nerfs are not an ornament added to the game, but the very means by which the ecosystem defines, in regular cycles, which characters and strategies remain competitively viable and which are, for a period, downgraded to the condition of suboptimal choices. In this key, the patch operates as a norm in operation. It does not merely readjust variables, but reconfigures, in practice, the competitive utility of the enjoyed assets, redistributes frequency of use, repositions preferences and alters the real “cost” of remaining in the environment, since what is functionally strong tends to concentrate attention, learning and investment of time.<1>p. 121</1>

If the meta is, to a large extent, the set of incentivized choices, then the update is not merely maintenance. It is the mechanism that makes functional obsolescence an ordinary component of enjoyment, since what was learned, mastered and chosen as an axis of performance can be downgraded, within weeks, by unilateral technical decision.<1>p. 122</1>

In publicly explaining its Champion Balance Framework, Riot Games describes the goal of making buff and nerf decisions “consistent” and “easier to understand”, including through measurable parameters, audience segmentation and combined use of win rate and ban rate, as well as thresholds that function as triggers for intervention <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2019a)</2>. The result is a technical rationality that presents itself as transparency and predictability, but that also fulfills a social function, insofar as it converts statistical performance into practical orders about what should be played, what should be avoided and what loses competitive centrality.<3>p. 122</3>

Riot maintains a public index of Patch Notes, in chronological sequence, which allows the regularity of the patch to be reconstructed as the normal mode of operation of the service <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2>.<3>p. 122</3>

Among the many practices consolidated by the company, the regular maintenance of the public index of patch notes is one of the most praiseworthy and was a mechanism by which the company adapted to the dialectical business model it had established with its community. The practice is, for most platforms, one of the most practical and functional ways of methodologically meeting the requirements of open auditability and maintenance of functional equivalence formulated in sections 5, 6 and 7 of this thesis.<1>p. 122</1>

The Terms of Service state that the supplier may alter, update, suspend and even “nerf” features and parts of the services, including virtual products, and they also provide for the application of background patches and automatic updates, with or without prior notice <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. Balancing presents itself, in this picture, as a regular exercise of governance by design: a mode of administering the ecosystem in which technical choices cyclically reorganize the field of the possible, modulate competitive utility and reorder incentives for remaining and acquiring.<3>p. 123</3>

In Section 5, dealing with the availability of virtual content, the text provides that “sometimes, we may change the purchasing power of Game Currency (for example, we may increase the number of Game Currency needed to buy Virtual Products, such as skins)” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. This reinforces the idea that the ecosystem is not merely a set of items, but an administered economy, in which value and access can be recalibrated by unilateral decision of the supplier.<3>p. 123</3>

The series Arcane, distributed by Netflix and produced with Riot's participation, extends the cultural centrality of characters and narratives, reaching audiences beyond the game and reinforcing the visibility of certain symbolic assets¹ <1>NETFLIX</1><2>(Netflix, 2024)</2>. From this perspective, the technical decision to introduce or reposition a character does not act on an abstract object, but on a figure whose meaning is continuously produced by cultural and marketing strategies.<3>p. 131</3>

The episode involving the champion Mel allows us to observe, more clearly, how the technical rationality of balancing can operate coupled to the symbolic economy of the ecosystem, without any need to attribute subjective intention to the decision-maker. The official introduction of the character was presented as a narrative and temporal milestone associated with the universe of Arcane, with an institutionally fixed release date <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025c)</2>.<3>p. 131-132</3>

The framing works as evidence that the technical decision to introduce a character comes with narrative and temporal marking, organizing collective expectation and attention in the ecosystem, as well as directly capitalizing, within the game, on the investment previously made in Arcane, since it is a character first introduced by the series and only afterward introduced to the game.<1>p. 132</1>
From then on, throughout 2025, the champion's presence remained at the center of governance by design for two complementary reasons.<1>p. 132</1>

First, her strength and the kind of defensive interaction her kit allowed became a recurring object of public evaluation and technical intervention, with effects on bans, frequency of appearance and perception of competitive legitimacy, which reveals that the meta does not “happen” only by collective preference, but is continuously administered by criteria and corrections. Second, already in the year-end cycle, this centrality was connected to a prestige window tied to rare cosmetic content, with a publicly recorded opening date <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025e)</2>. Then, in early 2026, patch 26.3 brought about a relevant respecification of the champion's mode of enjoyment by altering the central protection mechanism that sustained her interaction pattern, replacing the previous logic with a shield and expressly removing the damage immunity <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2026d)</4>.<5>p. 132</5>

Under patch 25.24, Riot records the release of prestige cosmetic content with a precise date: “Prestige Winterblessed Mel will be available December 3, 2025.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025e)</2>.<3>p. 132</3>

In patch 26.3, Riot qualifies the defensive change as a “big change”, recording: “One big change we have is changing her reflection damage immunity to a shield […]” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026d)</2>.<3>p. 132</3>
In the same patch, the modification appears objectively formalized in the ability description: “No longer grants damage immunity.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026d)</2>.<3>p. 132</3>

The sequence is sufficient to support the claim that design does not act only as technical optimization, but as social mediation that regulates centrality, acceptability and functional value, including when this regulation is synchronized with cycles of prestige and scarcity administered by the platform itself.<1>p. 132</1>

By defining which forms of protection will be allowed, which will be reconfigured and which interactions will be taken as excessively frustrating, design produces a policy incorporated into code, which governs the experience without presenting itself as an explicit legal norm. Therefore, balancing, although wrapped in the language of “game health”, operates as continuous administration of the environment, with the capacity to redistribute functional value and reorganize patterns of conduct and investment.<1>p. 132-133</1>

The record proves that there was an institutional offer window tied to rarity and recognition, which is relevant for characterizing the ecosystem's symbolic economy and its link to attention cycles.<1>p. 132</1>

The information suffices to show that the mechanism changed qualitatively, with the potential to bring about a change in the very practical expectation of enjoyment and in the functional stability of the acquired asset.<1>p. 132</1>

For the argument under discussion, this rules out simplifications, because the point is not to assert that platforms are only capture, but to demonstrate that capture can be produced by specific reorientations of functions that also sustain sociability, expression and collective organization. It is in this ambivalence that it becomes legally decisive to ask which teleologies were incorporated into the architecture and which conditions of auditability can make that incorporation open to criticism.<1>p. 136</1>

On its own, open auditability does not resolve the whole dispute, because demonstrating what changed and how it changed does not exhaust the question of the material legitimacy of the change.<1>p. 647</1>

It is precisely for this reason that, in dealing with the internet, Feenberg refuses to describe it as a neutral medium, since he insists that it is, above all, a technical system whose social meaning is inextricably intertwined with its technical character <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99)</2>.<3>p. 134</3>

The dispute around the internet, in this reading, is organized by competing models that Feenberg calls the “consumption model” and the “community model”. This polarization is useful for the study of digital consumption because it shows the contingency of the platform, since it does not result from an internal necessity of technique, but from conflicts between purposes and rationalities.<1>p. 134</1>

The distinction between the consumption model and the community model is especially productive for interactive entertainment because it shows how community resources (many-to-many communication, sociability and belonging) can be integrated into market rationality as an infrastructure of extraction. In other words, the community appears not only as a “social effect” of the product, but as part of its economic value and of its monetization architecture. This is central to understanding the concept of the IOC, because it confirms that the materiality of the object is relational and semiotic. Belonging, reputation and identity continuity are technically organized components, and not spontaneous externalities <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99-105)</2>.<3>p. 134-135</3>

The notion of concretization allows a more precise reading of the constitutive ambivalence of certain functionalities. A single technical structure can concentrate multiple purposes and serve public life and market life simultaneously, depending on how it is stabilized by the technical code <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99-105)</2>.<3>p. 136</3>

Feenberg observes that social networking sites serve commerce by serving community and that targeted advertising, based on data mining, constitutes a central source of revenue <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 105)</2>.<3>p. 136</3>

For the IOC regime, Feenberg reinforces two consequences. The first is that the materiality of the object is architectural and relational, because it depends on the technical form that stabilizes community and capture. The second is that the consumer's vulnerability must be read as factual vulnerability with a structural dimension under opaque ecosystems, in which the correspondence between expectation and delivery, between promise and enjoyment, is not immediately verifiable.<1>p. 136-137</1>

Technical rationality tends to expand as an organizing criterion of everyday life; media ecologies reformat what presents itself as reliable information, acceptable debate and relevant knowledge; and technique incorporated into routines fragments experience, reducing the density of the production of meaning and opening space for forms of symbolic steering that do not depend on explicit persuasion. Feenberg completes this picture by preventing the diagnosis from degrading into fatalism: technical rationality is institutionalized in concrete choices, stabilized in design, and therefore remains open to criticism, dispute and control.<1>p. 137</1>
In this scenario, “techno-media order” describes less a cultural background than a mode of practical coordination.<1>p. 137</1>
Even when there is no textual omission, steering can operate through curation and architecture, before reading and often outside it.<1>p. 138</1>

Digital consumption then emerges as insertion into continuous operational architectures. The consumer does not merely receive a final content. They come to inhabit an arrangement of access, curation, permissions, frictions and update cycles that exists while the system works and while the user remains integrated into it. The experience becomes inseparable from the conditions of its production. The consumed object takes on a relational and architectural form, since it is constituted by mediations that organize enjoyment, permanence, loss, modification and degradation over time.<1>p. 138</1>

Therefore, the consumption decision is rarely formed only by rational comparison of performance, price and adequacy. It is also organized by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging, in which value is staged, reiterated and stabilized by presentation formats.<1>p. 138</1>

Defaults, hierarchies of choice, recommendation systems, metrics and urgency devices produce an everyday grammar in which certain conducts are facilitated, others become improbable and many alternatives do not even appear as alternatives.<1>p. 138</1>

The vulnerability formed in this environment is not limited to a lack of information or to classic economic asymmetry. It bears on the capacity to interpret, verify and contest the very field in which the choice takes place. The decisive gap now opens between promise and the effective conditions of enjoyment, between sign and delivery, between the performance of belonging and the monetization infrastructure.<1>p. 138</1>
Terms and notices remain relevant, but they cease to be the main place where power is exercised.<1>p. 139</1>

The characterization of digital consumption as mediated and continued enjoyment finds support in Brazilian positive law, which already recognizes, in specific regulations tied to software and related services, duties of functional continuity and technical support linked to the economic exploitation of the object.<1>p. 91</1>

On platforms, this semiotic governance is reinforced by contracts, private moderation policies and proprietary infrastructures for the circulation of content. In this layer, intellectual property rights appear not only as protection of creations, but as a legal technology for controlling signs, delimiting uses and stabilizing expectations of enjoyment.<1>p. 91</1>

Seen in this light, contracts, private policies, technical standards and property regimes over signs and access appear as overlapping layers of a single governance. The offer is simultaneously narrative and infrastructure: it mobilizes belonging and recognition while administering visibility, repetition and reward.<1>p. 139</1>
What is permitted, encouraged or punished may be inscribed in interface, flow and metric, not only in a clause.<1>p. 138-139</1>

The question is no longer only the content of the promise and comes to include the way it becomes operative, as well as the mediations that shape enjoyment without letting themselves be fully verified by the addressee. This is the conceptual ground on which the teleology inscribed in design can be reconstructed as a structure of purpose and on which requirements such as auditability and functional value equivalence will come to operate as minimum parameters of legitimacy for exchanges mediated by systems.<1>p. 139</1>

Design rationality must be confronted as a material dimension of supply, preparing the following synthesis: the techno-media environment is not an external setting of the IOC, but its condition of possibility.<1>p. 137</1>

This point requalifies the usual language of the industry, which tends to hide the normative core under engineering vocabulary (“tweak”, “update”, “balancing”). When a platform unilaterally alters a rare cosmetic item or redesigns a character, it is determining, by code, the material conditions of enjoyment and the way the good will be recognized and compared in the social world of the game. If the alteration lowers the functional and symbolic value that motivated the acquisition, the problem is not “user nostalgia”, but an architectural redefinition of the content delivered, with a direct impact on auditability and on the attribution of abusiveness.<1>p. 135</1>

The Ellulian reference to “inevitability” must be taken as a critical description of a system effect, that is, of the tendency toward naturalization and self-justification of the technical, and not as a normative thesis according to which history would be closed to contestation.<1>p. 96</1>

Saying that technique acquires “autonomy” does not mean postulating a single, inevitable or monolithic causality, but recognizing that, in certain sociotechnical arrangements, institutional and economic incentives turn the innovation and implementation of systems into a partly self-fueling dynamic, frequently dissociated from public deliberation proportional to its effects. It is precisely in this space, between systemic tendency and the possibility of democratic governance, that the legal problem in question lies.<1>p. 88</1>

At the end of his work, Ellul questions the belief that technical progress is an objective synonym for human progress and makes an appeal to individual and collective responsibility in the face of technique <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 441-445)</2>.<3>p. 96</3>

Consumer Law cannot confine itself to checking clauses or isolated informational duties when experience, enjoyment and loss are conditioned by technical decisions embedded in the environment.<1>p. 137</1>

The first consequence is that design must be treated as a material dimension of supply, because the practical rules of access, permanence and loss that define the enjoyment of the immaterial object are stabilized in it. The second is that, if architecture concentrates teleologies and condenses ambivalent functions, legal control cannot depend only on general clauses or advertising promises, and must reach the mechanisms by which the platform produces equivalences, lowers values and applies modulations without sufficient transparency.<1>p. 137</1>
Postman's contribution matters not as nostalgia for print culture, but as a key to understanding that each medium sets up its own ecology of perception and knowledge.<1>p. 98</1>

By shifting rationality from the domain of an abstract ideal to that of an operating social function, Feenberg provides the bridge needed for the consumer law critique not to be confused with a moralizing refusal of technique. What is reconstructed is a regime of power whose effectiveness is produced by systems, standards and decision routines embedded in infrastructures <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 15-16)</2>.<3>p. 123</3>

For the purposes of this section, the reference does not anticipate the later dogmatic construction; it only shows that dependence on maintenance, updating and governance over time is not an accident external to the consumer relationship, but an attributable feature of supply in digital environments.<1>p. 91</1>
This problem does not turn every improvement into an unlawful act. Updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem.<1>p. 470</1>
Ellul is not summoned to support a generic critique of technological modernity, but to make intelligible the technical order in which the IOC is formed.<1>p. 97</1>
The conversion of public space into show business matters less for its sectoral object than for its mechanism.<1>p. 101</1>

Technical-operational modernity compresses dense symbolic mediations without eliminating the structural need for symbolization; it shifts, however, its supports and criteria of validity to artifacts, devices and functional grammars, opening space for metrics, performances and access infrastructures to take on, in practice, functions of belonging, validation and sanction comparable, by analogy, to those Durkheim describes in the symbolic regime, converting technical governance into lived moral routine.<1>p. 108</1>

The empirical dimension of the work is mobilized for an illustrative purpose and disciplined by mechanisms, so as to make intelligible institutional arrangements and legally relevant points of friction. There is no intention to describe the ecosystem exhaustively, nor to demonstrate statistical prevalence, nor to offer a complete overview of its history or its variations.<1>p. 49</1>

As to the status of the subsidiary use of collaborative repositories (such as Fandom) for naming categories and minimal operational description of mechanics, the criterion already set in Chapter 2 is adopted, according to which this material is not used to prove institutional promises, internal decision criteria or official milestones of change, operating only as technical-operational support and as a lead for locating primary documentation when this becomes necessary.<1>p. 94</1>

<1>The constitutional order and the sectoral framework</1>

The parameters of containment come from the CDC and the LGPD. Articles 8, 10 and 12 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> limit risks to those that are normal and foreseeable, bar products that the supplier knows or should know to have a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness and, in extreme cases, reopen the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product. Article 6, items I, III and VI, of Law 13,709/2018<3><4>2</4></3>, the General Data Protection Law (LGPD), requires a specific and informed purpose, necessity and transparency, subject to commercial and industrial secrets, and Articles 7, 8 and 46 of Law 13,709/2018<5><6>3</6></5> call for an adequate legal basis, consent that is not automatically satisfied by ritualized acceptances and security measures capable of protecting the data. The platform cannot invoke security as an all-encompassing justification while keeping the scope, the necessity and the agents of the processing opaque.

Sectoral regulation dismantles two simplifications, the notion that the sector would be legally invisible and the notion that naming it in a statute would be enough to resolve the conflicts of its governance. Articles 1, 2 and 5 of Law 14,852/2024<1><2>4</2></1> create the legal framework for the electronic games industry, regulate its economic chain and define what an electronic game is, and Articles 11 and 12 of Law 14,852/2024<3><4>5</4></3> treat the sector as innovation and culture. This recognition reinforces that games operated as a service are ecosystems of continuous operation, and it coexists with recurring concerns about vulnerable audiences, microtransactions, random mechanisms, personal data and integrated advertising, which are typical effects of these ecosystems rather than accidents.

The recognition comes framed as regulated economic freedom. Article 3 of Law 14,852/2024<1><2>6</2></1> declares the activity free, subject to Article 173 of the Constitution<3><4>7</4></3>, and requires the age rating to take into account the risks of microtransactions, the purchases that, in games as a service, tend to occur continuously and in segments within enjoyment itself. Article 6, items IV, V, VI and VII, of Law 14,852/2024<5><6>8</6></5> lists among its principles fundamental rights, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents and data protection, which rules out any legal infantilization of the problem. The sole paragraph of Article 5 of Law 14,852/2024<7><8>9</8></7> excludes games involving betting or with a random or forecast-based outcome from the definition of electronic game, and nothing follows from this about loot boxes. The framework also added the registration of games to Article 2, item VI, of Law 9,279/1996<9><10>10</10></9>, the Industrial Property Law, which makes it even more necessary to contain the proprietarian temptation to capture conflicts that, on the plane of enjoyment, remain conflicts of governed consumption.

The law affirms the freedom to manufacture, import, market, develop and commercially use electronic games, but does so with express reference to Article 173 of the Constitution<1><2>7</2></1> and to current legislation. This is relevant because the framework does not enshrine a sectoral free-for-all disguised as friendly modernity.<3>p. 544</3>

“Art. 3 The manufacturing, importation, commercialization, development and commercial use of electronic games are free, subject to the provisions of Art. 173 of the Federal Constitution<1><2>11</2></1> and of current legislation. § 1 The State shall carry out the indicative age rating, prior state authorization being waived for the development and exploitation of the electronic games covered by this Law. § 2 In carrying out the indicative age rating of electronic games, the risks related to the use of microtransaction mechanisms shall be taken into account.” <3>Brasil</3><4>(Brasil, [2024]b)</4>.<5>p. 544</5>

Law 15,211/2025, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents, matters as evidence, because it shows that these mechanics have already been identified as structurally sensitive. Article 5 of Law 15,211/2025<1><2>12</2></1> imposes duties of prevention, protection, information and security in line with the best interest of the child, Article 20 of Law 15,211/2025<3><4>13</4></3> prohibits loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents, and also in those likely to be accessed by this audience, and Article 22 of Law 15,211/2025<5><6>14</6></5> prohibits profiling for commercial advertising. The regime is not lax, since Articles 29 and 40 of Law 15,211/2025<7><8>15</8></7> require the removal of content that violates rights and a legal representative in the country, and Articles 1 to 3 of Decree 12,622/2025<9><10>16</10></9> make the National Data Protection Agency the administrative authority and provide for blocking orders. Its entry into force was brought forward to March 2026, which reveals a concrete regulatory problem rather than a symbolic agenda.
